article_text:
John Carpenter getting a major honor from the ACE Eddie Awards is a Thing.

In a move perfectly timed for Halloween week, American Cinema Editors said Wednesday that celebrated horrormeister will receive its 2027 ACE Golden Eddie Filmmaker of the Year award.

The filmmaker behind the original Halloween , The Fog, The Thing, They Live and so many others including Escape from New York and Escape from L.A. will be feted during the 77th annual ACE Eddie Awards on February 7 at UCLA’s Royce Hall . Comic and actor Patton Oswalt is back to host the ceremony.

“John Carpenter makes movies that get under your skin and stay there,” ACE President Sabrina Plisco said. “ Halloween , The Thing , Escape from New York — these films have scared, thrilled and shaped generations of audiences and filmmakers alike. Few directors understand rhythm, tension and restraint the way he does, and he has always trusted his editors to help him find it. That collaboration is exactly what this honor celebrates.”

RELATED: Top 50 Classic Horror Movies

The honorary society also revealed that Bonnie Koehler and Christopher Nelson will receive Career Achievement awards during the show, which celebrates outstanding editing in film, television, documentaries, shorts and digital content.

“Bonnie Koehler and Chris Nelson are editors other editors look up to,” Plisco said. “Bonnie went from American Zoetrope to an Emmy nomination for L.A. Law and an ACE Eddie nomination for Law & Order: Special Victims Unit , television’s longest-running primetime drama. Chris cut the finale of Lost , one of the most watched and debated hours in television history, and his work on Six Feet Under and Mad Men helped define prestige television. Both have given generously to our community.”

RELATED: 10 Terrifyingly Good Horror Triple Bills To Watch This Halloween

Nominees in 14 categories for the 2027 ACE Eddie Awards will be revealed on Thursday, January 14. Back in February, eventual Best Picture Oscar winner One Battle After Another and its 2026 awards season rival Sinners took the top film prizes at the 76th Eddie Awards . Andy Jurgensen also won the Academy Award for Best Editing. Toon juggernaut KPop Demon Hunters won the animation prize en route to the Best Animated Feature Oscar.

article_text:
The red-feathered hero of “ The Angry Birds Movie 3 ” looks reassuringly familiar, but DNEG Animation had to rebuild much of him to bring the franchise back to theaters. And as the studio reconstructed Red’s fur, facial rig and expressions, it also developed a system that ultimately automated character-effects work on roughly 75% of the film’s shots.

“He’s similar by choice,” VFX supervisor Patrick Harboun said at View Conference in Turin on Friday.

The upcoming Paramount release, directed by John Rice, reunites Jason Sudeikis’ Red with Silver, voiced by Rachel Bloom, as they navigate parenthood alongside their latest adventure. DNEG takes over animation duties from the Sony Pictures Animation productions behind the first two films.

The technical handover was anything but straightforward. In fact, proprietary grooming, rigging and surfacing tools used on the predecessors could not simply be transferred to DNEG’s pipeline. “We had to start from this. A plucked chicken version of Red,” Harboun joked, displaying a bare digital model. Even its underlying geometry needed reworking before the team could reconstruct its feathers.

The result deliberately avoided a radical makeover. Red’s plumage became slightly softer, while his eyes and beak gained firmer, more toy-like surfaces. “Once an IP becomes popular, it kind of belongs to the fans, and we have to respect that,” Harboun said. “We can’t just add our own spin just to give our mark.”

The studio scrutinized the earlier movies frame by frame. “We analyzed the past movies to find the unwritten rules of animation,” he explained. Animators cataloged the angles of Red’s beak, the geometry of his narrowed eyes and the boundaries beyond which a stretched expression stopped feeling like Red. The lessons became a style guide and a reusable library of facial expressions.

There was more room for experimentation with over 20 new characters, including Red and Silver’s children: aspiring athlete Glider, voiced by Walker Scobell; temperamental June, played by Emma Myers; and baby Olly, voiced by Psalm West. The family also has a pet spider named Fuzzy, voiced by James Austin Johnson. “The goal was to make a spider that even an arachnophobe would love,” Harboun said.

Olly created a distinctive technical challenge because his glasses effectively serve as animated eyes, complete with moving eyelids and brows. DNEG’s solution, nicknamed “Pancake Eyes,” involved duplicating and flattening portions of the baby’s facial rig behind the lenses, then restoring curvature and allowing the expressions to respond to the character’s exaggerated squash-and-stretch movement.

The biggest efficiency gain came through a performance-effects process building on DNEG’s earlier work for “The Garfield Movie.” Following approval of a character’s animation, the system automatically simulated selected effects on fur, feathers and deformation, rendered a preview and identified shots requiring bespoke artist attention. As the crew encountered new problems, they improved reusable templates for each character.

“It’s not machine learning, it’s human learning,” Harboun underlined, stressing that artists maintained those templates. Early in production, around 25% of shots could pass through the automated process; by later stages, that figure had risen to 75%. “This frees up a lot of artists for hero work,” he explained. The percentage applies to character-effects processing, not to shots being animated or completed without artists.

Other inventions included a secondary, normally invisible layer of fur that appears when characters stretch, preventing bald patches, and one-click tools for building ropes, hay and props that animators could manipulate independently, without repeatedly calling on other departments.

Production designer Jeanie Chang’s saturated tropical palette posed another challenge. Lighting references were painted directly over layout images so artists could match intended compositions, but differently colored characters still required individual lighting adjustments within the same scene. “In every given situation, Red always needs to be red,” Harboun said.

The film also expands Bird Island with Pigtropolis, a city for its pig residents. Harboun revealed that the opening sequence was changed from night to day late in production. He encouraged audiences to seek out the 3D version when the film opens Dec. 23: “I’m usually not a fan of 3D, but I really recommend that you check out the 3D version.”

For Harboun, such innovations only work when they reinforce what audiences already recognize. The characters may have been rebuilt and their workflows reinvented, but their familiar identities remain the foundation.

解説・あらすじ

article_text:
Verve has signed a new 10-year lease for its worldwide headquarters in the Hollywood Media District, marking a significant commitment to the Los Angeles entertainment economy.

Located across from Sunset Las Palmas Studios, Verve’s HQ is situated alongside companies including Netflix, All3Media, Formosa Group, Paramount, SiriusXM and Roc Nation.

Verve commissioned global design collective RIOS to design a headquarters that reflects the agency’s independent culture and ambitions. Its ground-floor theater serves as a meeting place for screenings, press events, conversations with executives and filmmakers and other industry and community programming.

Intentionally making Verve’s long-term home here reflects who we are as advocates for creative talent invested in the future of our industry and the community that drives it. This investment launches Verve’s next decade with the mandate that has defined us from the start: to deliver truly client-first representation built around each client’s individuality and ambition.”

Popular on Variety

Founded in 2010, Verve is an independent talent and literary agency with operational divisions spanning motion picture literary, television literary, talent, non-fiction, media rights & publishing, Verve Ventures, commercial endorsements and digital. Verve clients include actors like Matthew Lillard, Keith David, Sean Bean, Olivia Thirlby and Eliza Coupe and filmmakers like Sara Hess, Ben Leonberg, Zeb Wells and Adam Stein.

article_text:
Feature

How Art Can Deliver Justice for Refugees

In the legal system, art created by refugees and incarcerated people can serve both as a form of therapy and as evidence of mass atrocities.

Enayet Khan fled Myanmar in 2017. For three days, he moved through forests and fields with his family, slipping from one village to the next as fires closed in behind them. Each time they stopped, the safety was temporary — by morning, that village too would be burning. His own home had already been reduced to ash, but there was no time to mourn what was lost. Armed soldiers moved quickly, and Khan saw people being shot in front of him. The goal was simple : to survive long enough to find a way out of Myanmar. Ten members of his family fled together; three were injured along the way. Eventually, they crossed the border into Bangladesh.

“I lost everything,” Khan told Hyperallergic in a phone call. “Home, documentation, property, a sense of security.”

Khan settled in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, now home to nearly one million Rohingya refugees. The Rohingya people have endured decades of discrimination and repression under Myanmar’s successive governments. Stripped of citizenship by a 1982 law, they remain one of the largest stateless groups in the world. Most fled in 2017 to escape the military’s crimes against humanity and genocide .

In the camps, Khan turned to painting and drawing to process the atrocities he had witnessed: burning homes, fleeing families, and executions. Over time, he began training other refugees to do the same, establishing the Rohingya Art Club (RAC) and encouraging visual storytelling as a form of expression and resistance.

Khan is one of many refugees using art to record experiences of conflict and violence. According to legal experts, such work can also play a role in accountability efforts, helping to convey testimony and corroborate survivor accounts, and even enter legal proceedings as evidence of mass atrocities.

A record 117.8 million people have been forcibly displaced worldwide — a number that has risen for 12 consecutive years. Investigations and prosecutions of genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes have surged within the European Union, with new cases increasing by 44% between 2016 and 2021. Today, more displaced people are turning to international courts to hold perpetrators accountable, an increase in demand that the International Criminal Court (ICC) itself has called “ unprecedented .”

For some legal advocates, art has become one way to meet that demand.

Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide and a former United Nations investigator, collected artwork as part of the evidence in a case before the International Court of Justice that charged the Myanmar military with genocide against Rohingya communities in 2017. She noted that the high illiteracy rate among Rohingya people, especially women and children, makes it difficult to record traditional statements. In those contexts, drawings became a vital way to convey their testimonies.

article_text:
A Frieze Masters 2026 , una nuova prospettiva attraversa le gallerie della fiera londinese. Si chiama Queering Modernism: Visual Languages of the 20th Century ed è il settore curatoriale curato da Anke Kempkes per esplorare le rappresentazioni queer nell’arte del Novecento. Non una storia parallela, ma un invito a rileggere quella che già conosciamo, facendo emergere identità, desideri e sperimentazioni spesso trascurati dalla critica. E dalla storia dell’arte.

«Una delle storie nascoste – benché sotto gli occhi di tutti», scrive Kempkes, riguarda proprio le pratiche artistiche attraverso cui identità non conformi e modi di vivere alternativi hanno conquistato visibilità, in contesti segnati da censura ed esclusione. Il progetto nasce da qui: dalla possibilità di riconoscere nuovi significati nelle opere e di mettere in discussione le categorie con cui il modernismo è stato tramandato.

Il percorso si sviluppa attraverso presentazioni di diverse gallerie. Alberta Pane Gallery accosta le fotografie di Marcel Moore, dedicate alla sua compagna Claude Cahun, all’opera della pioniera femminista Judy Chicago. Nei ritratti e nelle autorappresentazioni di Cahun, l’identità diventa una materia mobile, sottratta a definizioni rigide. Da Galerie Albrecht, la fotografia di Ruth Bernhard esplora invece il nudo femminile attraverso forme essenziali e suggestioni surrealiste.

Un altro nucleo è quello presentato congiuntamente da Victoria Miro e David Zwirner, dedicato ad Alice Neel, celebre per i suoi ritratti diretti di artisti, intellettuali, attivisti e performer gender non-conforming della New York del secondo Novecento. La sua pittura restituisce ai soggetti una presenza irriducibile alle convenzioni sociali.

Lo sguardo si allarga oltre l’Europa e gli Stati Uniti con Ismael Nery, presentato da Danielian. Nelle opere del modernista brasiliano, figure androgine e identità sdoppiate aprono uno spazio di riflessione sulla fluidità del genere. Ab-Anbar Gallery presenta invece Bahman Mohassess, artista iraniano la cui ricerca intreccia dissenso, esilio e provocazione, mettendo in relazione il linguaggio artistico con le tensioni politiche del proprio tempo. E poi ancora Glyn Philpot e Lotte Laserstein, presentati da Agnews , e Luis Fernando Zapata, le cui sculture e forme rituali, esposte da Elvira Moreno Gallery e Alonso Garcés Galería, affrontano la mortalità e la memoria.

A tenere insieme queste esperienze non è uno stile comune, ma la loro capacità di sfidare le classificazioni. Con Queering Modernism , Frieze Masters crea un inedito itinerario tra le gallerie: un’occasione per scoprire figure meno note e osservare artisti affermati da angolazioni nuove. La posta in gioco non è soltanto recuperare ciò che è stato dimenticato, ma ampliare lo sguardo sul modernismo e sulla pluralità delle esperienze che lo hanno attraversato.

in camera galerie , Les Rencontres du Sud and Ciné Club Afro are organizing a private screening of Ananias Léki Dago ’s documentary Je reste photographe ( I am still a photographer) , on the occasion of the exhibition Paul Kodjo: Photoromance at the Palais de Tokyo.

In Je reste photographe , Ananias Léki Dago looks back at the preservation work undertaken to save photographer Paul Kodjo’s negatives. Beyond the portrait of an artist, the film opens a reflection on the conservation of African photographic archives and the place they occupy in our collective memory.

Tuesday, October 27 8 p.m. UGC Odéon (124 bd Saint-Germain, Paris 6th) Admission is free with reservation, subject to availability. RSVP link.

The screening will be followed by a discussion with the director, moderated by journalist Samba Doucoure.

This event is organized with the support of the Ministry of Culture and Francophonie of Côte d’Ivoire.

"问题在于数字艺术究竟是什么，以及它希望如何被体验。从本质上讲，数字空间没有固定的形体或形式。它存在于数字抽象之中，其表征大多由光、声、数据和时间构成。它不再栖息于独特、单一的空间实体中；我认为它存在于我更愿意将其描述为环境的东西中，活在重叠和连接之中，其中一种状态随时可以融入另一种状态。然而，数字艺术大体上仍然在继承自其他媒介的空间、在神经质孤立的房间中展出。我想创造一个更具环境感的空间，它分享着数字本身的流动性，在这里，体验不会在明确的门槛处停止并重新开始，而是随着你的移动不断展开。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在融美术馆，问题在于建筑如何帮助塑造一个机构及其在一个快速增长的城市中的角色。寿城则完全不同。它的尺度本地且亲密，扎根于一个社区及其公园。美术馆的动线提供了逐渐变化的内部和外部条件，而没有规定每一处必须是什么样。它通过它将容纳的艺术品以及走过其中的人们向公众开放并接受解读。", "paragraph", "text": "正如你所观察到的那样，数字艺术繁荣于重叠和持续的转变，而非孤立。ZKM | 艺术与媒体中心作为你家乡卡尔斯鲁厄的开创性机构，也是该项目的合作者。与他们合作，以及或许你对该机构自身的记忆，是如何帮助将这种新媒体逻辑转化为建筑形式的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ZKM Copyright and courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren.", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你曾说过，建筑应该预见其中将要发生的生活，并摆脱你所称的现代主义信条“形式遵循功能”那“有害的束缚”。在一个没有房间或门廊的美术馆里，你将如何编排参观者的动线，让氛围在过渡时逐渐流转，而不是在门槛处戛然而止或发生突变？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Suseong Continuum》的核心理念是一个空间渐变过程，其中变化是连续发生的，一种状态会演变成另一种状态。传统的门槛消融在对数字空间更具连续性的理解中。随着你的移动，光线、声音、围合感和沉浸感都在逐渐变化。曲折的墙壁在宽阔处化为开阔的空间，在狭窄处收紧为通道。氛围在不断转化，而非瞬间切换。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "材料同样承载着这段旅程。在外部，混凝土质感粗糙，脚下踩着碎石。在内部，表面逐渐变得平滑洁白，专为数字投影而校准，地面则换成了抛光混凝土。沿途你会经历沉思、相遇和完全沉浸的状态，而作品之间从不完全孤立。它们既可以构成一个连续的整体，也可以各自占据路径的不同部分。我喜欢这种模糊性。它不强加任何一种单一的解读方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/16/43/16435400-f27e-4b41-b5f7-d0c24f5ce4de/content/images/2026/10/Suseong-Continuum-by-Ole-Scheeren----Buro-OS_03-1.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtAsiaPacific", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "OLE SCHEEREN . Project imagery by Büro Ole Scheeren. Copyright and courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren.", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着媒体技术的飞速演进，你将如何确保《Suseong Continuum》在数十年里依然保持生命力？这其中的宏愿是否包含某种建筑学上的永恒性，而将持久的混凝土外壳与灵活的技术层相分离又是如何支撑这一愿景的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "建筑的寿命通常比其内部的技术更长，因此我对时间的兴趣在于理解变化并预见新的可能性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于这座美术馆，你可以从两种时间来思考。实体混凝土外壳关乎持久：耐用、坚固，扎根于大地并承载着场地的记忆。技术层则是短暂的：投影、声音和各种系统，可以随着艺术的需求随时更换和重塑。我们将该层设计为贯穿整条路径的隐藏基础设施，电力、数据和安装点都隐蔽在天花板和地板中，但在时间推移中依然触手可及且可更换。对于参观者而言，它们几乎不可见，因此体验始终保持为纯粹的空间与氛围。对于技术人员而言，它们完全可接近，从而让艺术家和策展人能够快速重新配置美术馆。从某种意义上说，这座建筑不必去预测 30 年后的数字艺术会是什么样子。它只需对艺术保持开放，并允许各种可能性不断展开。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Elaine W. Courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In March, ArtAsiaPacific joined architect Ole Scheeren on a walkthrough of the Róng Museum of Art , an ambitious new home for visual and digital culture taking shape in Shenzhen. Barely seven months later, the founder of Büro Ole Scheeren has unveiled a very different proposition: a low-lying, partly sunken gallery for digital media art in Suseong, a residential district in southeast Daegu. Named Suseong Continuum, the project was commissioned for the Suseong International Biennale. Unlike conventional biennials that favor ephemeral pavilions, the event invites architects, landscape designers, and urban planners to create permanent civic infrastructure across Daegu—part of a long-term effort to give the city a stronger cultural identity. Scheeren’s proposal is on view at this year’s edition, “Living Ground,” through November 22. Construction begins in 2027, with the building scheduled to welcome visitors for the 2028 Biennale. Although best known for high-rises and mixed-use complexes, Scheeren has routinely worked across scales. In Suseong, he adopts a deliberately modest one: a single low structure emerges from a neighborhood park beside a lotus pond, its coarse concrete exterior giving way to a pale, screen-ready interior with no partitions to interrupt the visitor’s journey. The ambition is less about making a landmark than about rethinking how people encounter art composed of light and data. Yet digital art is still mostly shown in spaces inherited from other media, in neutral isolated chambers. I wanted to create a more ambient space that shares the fluidity of the digital itself, where an experience doesn’t stop and restart at distinct thresholds but keeps unfolding as you move."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the Róng Museum of Art, the question was how architecture could help shape an institution and its role in a rapidly growing city. Ole Scheeren on the Suseong Continuum

OLE SCHEEREN . Photo by Raymond Chen. Courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren.

In March, ArtAsiaPacific joined architect Ole Scheeren on a walkthrough of the Róng Museum of Art , an ambitious new home for visual and digital culture taking shape in Shenzhen. Barely seven months later, the founder of Büro Ole Scheeren has unveiled a very different proposition: a low-lying, partly sunken gallery for digital media art in Suseong, a residential district in southeast Daegu. Named Suseong Continuum, the project was commissioned for the Suseong International Biennale. Unlike conventional biennials that favor ephemeral pavilions, the event invites architects, landscape designers, and urban planners to create permanent civic infrastructure across Daegu—part of a long-term effort to give the city a stronger cultural identity. Scheeren’s proposal is on view at this year’s edition, “Living Ground,” through November 22. Construction begins in 2027, with the building scheduled to welcome visitors for the 2028 Biennale. Although best known for high-rises and mixed-use complexes, Scheeren has routinely worked across scales. In Suseong, he adopts a deliberately modest one: a single low structure emerges from a neighborhood park beside a lotus pond, its coarse concrete exterior giving way to a pale, screen-ready interior with no partitions to interrupt the visitor’s journey. The ambition is less about making a landmark than about rethinking how people encounter art composed of light and data. In this interview, Scheeren reflects on how a Korean tree found its way into the building’s surfaces, why a long dialogue with the Center for Art and Media (ZKM) Karlsruhe helped shape the gallery’s logic, how the formative late-1990s exhibition “Cities on the Move” in Southeast Asia still informs his practice, and whether architecture can keep pace with art forms that have yet to be invented.

OLE SCHEEREN . Project imagery by Büro Ole Scheeren. Copyright and courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren.

OLE SCHEEREN . Project imagery by Büro Ole Scheeren. Copyright and courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren.

Your buildings have long treated the city as a living organism. With Suseong Continuum, you seem to want to dissolve the boundary building and terrain. How did the site at Yeonhonae-ji, set between park, lotus pond, and mountains, shape this thinking?

Rather than dissolving, I see it more as a continuation, as a form of spatial gradient. The idea is to form a gradual transition from landscape to architecture, and from the physical reality of nature to the virtual world of a gallery dedicated to digital art.

A single meandering path winds through the park and materializes as the volume of the gallery. It twists, expands, and contracts in response to the triangular shape of the site, the pond, and the park’s pathways, and it negotiates the changing levels of the terrain as a means of tying everything together. You don’t arrive at the building so much as find yourself already inside it, still walking the same path you started in the park.

The gallery is partly embedded in the earth, which naturally stabilizes its internal temperature against the hot summers and cold winters of the local climate. Its solid concrete walls are imprinted with timber formwork made from the pine trees found in abundance locally. In Korea, the pine carries deep cultural significance as a symbol of integrity and longevity.

OLE SCHEEREN . Project imagery by Büro Ole Scheeren. Copyright and courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren.

When we met in March during a site visit to the Róng Museum, you spoke of designing as a “layering of possibilities.” Here, that possibility appears again, as something digital rather than institutional. What led you to abandon the sequential logic of the conventional contemporary art museum and its white cube format, and instead treat the gallery as one continuous spatial experience?

The question is what digital art is really about, and how it wants to be experienced. In essence, digital space has no fixed body or form. It exists in numeric abstraction, and its representations are mostly made of light, sound, data, and time. It no longer inhabits distinct, singular spatial entities; I think it exists in what I would rather describe as environments, living in overlaps and connections where one condition can merge into the next at any time. Yet digital art is still mostly shown in spaces inherited from other media, in neutral isolated chambers. I wanted to create a more ambient space that shares the fluidity of the digital itself, where an experience doesn’t stop and restart at distinct thresholds but keeps unfolding as you move.

At the Róng Museum of Art, the question was how architecture could help shape an institution and its role in a rapidly growing city. Suseong is something quite different. It is local and intimate in scale, rooted in a neighborhood and its park. The gallery’s movements offer gradually changing internal and external conditions without prescribing what each one has to be. It is open to interpretation through the artworks it will host and the people who walk through it.

Digital renderings of the interior of the Suseong Continuum, Daegu, by OLE SCHEEREN . Project imagery by Büro Ole Scheeren. Copyright and courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren.

Digital art, as you have observed, thrives on overlap and continual transformation rather than isolation. ZKM | Center for Art and Media, a pioneering institution in your home city of Karlsruhe, is also a collaborator on this project. How did working with them, and perhaps your own memories of the institution, help translate that new media logic into architectural form?

ZKM was one of the first institutions globally to formally recognize media as an art form. It treated art, science, and technology as one continuous field rather than separate disciplines, an approach very close to how I think about our architecture for this gallery.

Our dialogue with ZKM has given a strong focus to the interpretation and possible representation of media art: how it is conceived, how it behaves, and how it is constantly reinvented. With Suseong Continuum, we translated this into a spatial experience: how people move, observe, interact, and remember.

OLE SCHEEREN . Project imagery by Büro Ole Scheeren. Copyright and courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren.

Beyond ZKM, which museums or cultural institutions focused on new media and digital art, in Asia or elsewhere, shaped your thinking as you developed the proposal for Suseong’s continuous spatial model? Were there particular spatial strategies or curatorial approaches you sought to expand or move beyond?

In 1999, I worked with the curators Hans Ulrich Obrist and Hou Hanru on “Cities on the Move,” a large-scale exhibition about the Asian city. After touring museums and galleries in the West, it moved to Bangkok, where, instead of staying within the walls of a single museum, it became an urban intervention. We spread the show across the city through a network of institutional, academic, and alternative spaces, indoors and out, with artworks woven into everyday urban life. The central question of its scenography was not simply how to accommodate a series of artworks, but how to merge them with their actual context—the city, which was the very subject of its curatorial interest. I have been exploring these themes ever since: how art and its contexts relate, which conditions particular forms of art engage, and what idea of space we can derive from them.

OLE SCHEEREN . Project imagery by Büro Ole Scheeren. Copyright and courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren.

You have said that architecture should anticipate the lives it will contain and move away from what you have called the “detrimental straitjacket” of the modernist mantra “form follows function.” In a gallery without rooms or doorways, how will you choreograph visitors’ journeys so that the atmosphere shifts gradually rather than abruptly at a threshold?

The core idea of Suseong Continuum is a spatial gradient in which change happens continuously and one condition morphs into the next. Traditional thresholds dissolve into a more continuous understanding of digital space. Light, sound, enclosure, and immersion shift gradually as you move. Curving walls widen into open spaces and tighten into passages. Atmospheres transform rather than switch.

Materials carry that journey too. Outside, the concrete is rough and you walk on gravel. Inside, the surfaces slowly become smoother and whiter, calibrated for digital projection, and the floor becomes polished concrete. Along the route, you pass through states of contemplation, encounter, and full immersion without the works ever being completely isolated from one another. They can form one continuous condition, but can also occupy different sections of the path individually. I like that ambiguity. It doesn’t impose one way of reading.

OLE SCHEEREN . Project imagery by Büro Ole Scheeren. Copyright and courtesy Büro Ole Scheeren.

With media technology evolving so rapidly, how are you ensuring Suseong Continuum remains relevant over the decades? Is the ambition a form of architectural timelessness, and how does separating a durable concrete shell from a flexible technical layer support this vision?

Buildings generally outlive the technologies inside them, so what interests me about time is understanding change and anticipating new possibilities.

For the gallery, you can think of two kinds of time. The physical concrete shell is about endurance: durable, robust, embedded in the earth and carrying the memory of the site. The technical layer is ephemeral: projections, sound, and systems that can be replaced and reinvented as often as the art demands. We designed that layer as hidden infrastructure running along the entire path, with power, data, and mounting points concealed in ceilings and floors but accessible and replaceable over time. For visitors it is almost invisible, so the experience remains one of pure space and atmosphere. For technicians, it is fully accessible, so artists and curators can reconfigure the gallery quickly. In a way, the building doesn’t have to predict what digital art will look like in 30 years. It only has to stay open to it and allow diverse possibilities to unfold.

Elaine W. Ng is editor and publisher of ArtAsiaPacific.

The artist discusses his new commission, The Form of Light , for Bvlgari’s current exhibition in Shanghai.

Canvas: What can you tell us about your commissioned work for Bvlgari Kaleidos: Colors, Cultures and Crafts?

Zhang Ding: The Form of Light consists of an immersive light installation composed of two sets of golden light panels and glass humanoid heads with pixelated effects, all animated by light fluctuations.

What inspired the concept?

It was inspired by urban contemporary landscapes and new technology devices, and their inextricable presence in our society.

Why did you choose the title The Form of Light ?

A strong golden light emanates from the work, flickering and varying as if breathing. Here light becomes the essence of the work, immaterial yet immersive, infusing a spiritual dimension into the piece.

How does the gold light impact the perception of space?

The variations in light from dim to bright can sometimes be almost blinding to the eye, such as sunlight, while creating heat.

What is the significance of using the colour gold?

Gold – and its countless symbols – is a recurrent element in my practice. In this work specifically, it could be interpreted as a spiritual glow.

Are there any other colours that hold a special significance to you?

In my past works, I also repeatedly used phosphorescent green, for its ghostly luminescence.

What do the transparent glass humanoid heads suggest? How does the gemstone-like surface interact with the installation?

With their futuristic aesthetics, the glass humanoid heads are reminiscent of robotic heads. Simultaneously, their sharp shapes and translucency echo gemstones and the way they reflect light.

Do you see the light as spiritual, natural, technological or something else?

All of those. Light – as with gold – holds so many symbols and is intimately linked to human civilisation. The work plays on this dichotomy between natural and man-made.

Why did you choose to work with glass and light? What about these materials speaks to you?

Both elements represent a form of purity and resonate with the glow of gemstones.

How does this work expand on your current practice?

The work is part of a body of installations I have been working on these last few years, probing developments in new technology, their background and impact on our society.

What does Kaleidos mean to you? How does your work with Bvlgari expand on the exploration of colour and light?

The term Kaleidos brings to my mind multiple light, colours and geometrical structures, as well as the multifaceted perspectives of our reality.

Source: Still from ‘The Ghost Of Peter Sellers’ / Christopher Sharman

Peter Medak

Peter Medak, the UK-Hungarian director of The Changeling , The Krays and The Ruling Class , has died in Los Angeles. He was 88.

Medak was born in Budapest, Hungary, in 1937 and developed a fascination for filmmaking at the age of eight when his aunt gave him a 35mm hand-cranked projector and a strip of film.

After the family had been forced into hiding during the Second World War, Medak and his family endured further hardship under post-war Communist rule when his father was classified as a capitalist and imprisoned and his brother died. With his mother away for much of the day working in a plastics factory, the young Medak had time on his hands.

“I became an observer, you know, looking through this incredible keyhole of our apartment,” Medak once recalled. “I kept going seeing the same movies, three, four times a day. I started very early on, dissecting them – strange kind of propaganda films – you begin to see how it all kind of works.”

Medak consumed books, plays, films and music and at the age of 18 he fled to England in 1956 during the Hungarian Uprising against the communist regime. Barely able to speak a word of English, he got work through the industry connections of his opera-singer aunt Lotte Medák, training at British Pathe and then working on the sets of British productions at Elstree, Pinewood and Shepperton studios.

He worked as an assistant director on The Great Armored Car Swindle (1961, aka The Breaking Point ) and The Phantom Of The Opera (1962) before MCA Universal Pictures brought him to Los Angeles in 1963 and he signed a television-directing contract to work on the series Court Martial .

In 1967, Paramount signed him to direct his first feature, Negatives , starring Glenda Jackson. He went on to direct the stage adaptations A Day In The Death Of Joe Egg (1972) with Alan Bates and The Ruling Class (1972) with Peter O’Toole, which premiered in Cannes and garnered a lead actor Oscar nomination for O’Toole.

Over six decades, Medak directed 27 features, among them The Changeling (1980) with George C. Scott; The Krays (1990); Let Him Have It (1991); and Romeo Is Bleeding (1993), with Gary Oldman. His 2018 documentary The Ghost Of Peter Sellers was Medak’s account of a low point – his ill-fated 1973 pirate comedy Ghost In The Noonday Sun at Columbia Pictures. Production was nearly derailed by his friend Sellers’ eccentric behaviour and a spiralling budget and the film never reached the silver screen.

Medak’s prolific television work saw him direct episodes on such acclaimed series as The Wire , Breaking Bad , Homicide: Life On The Street and Chicago Hope . He also directed music videos for the likes of Peter Gabriel and Pink Floyd, and shot a production of Salome In Minneapolis and Rigoletto with Los Angeles Opera.

Medak once said: “If it’s in your blood, directing, you never stop directing and it doesn’t matter that you’re alone in your mind, dreaming or imagining things but you’re always making a movie.”

A devoted family man, he is survived by his four children Christopher, Joshua, Karen and Cornelia Medak; and his five grandchildren Sacha, Marlowe, Ryden, Oliver and Anders.

He was married to Katherine La Kermance, Carolyn Seymour and Julia Migenes, and was in a relationship with Christine Wagner.

Nel 2026 la Fondazione Palazzo Strozzi festeggia vent’anni di attività e sceglie di ripercorrere la propria storia guardando anche alle prospettive future: l’appuntamento è per venerdì 27 novembre, alle ore 17.30, al Teatro del Maggio Musicale Fiorentino. L’evento sarà pubblico e vedrà la partecipazione di Jeff Koons e JR , in dialogo con Arturo Galansino , Direttore Generale della Fondazione.

L’incontro, intitolato Vent’anni di Fondazione Palazzo Strozzi 2006-2026 , sarà introdotto dagli interventi del Presidente della Fondazione Luigi De Siervo e dello stesso Galansino e l’ingresso sarà gratuito ma con prenotazione obbligatoria fino a esaurimento dei posti disponibili. La presenza dei due artisti offrirà l’occasione di tornare su alcuni dei progetti che hanno segnato la programmazione dell’istituzione fiorentina, con Jeff Koons che è stato protagonista della mostra Jeff Koons. Shine e JR che ha realizzato La Ferita , monumentale installazione concepita per la facciata di Palazzo Strozzi.

Dal 2006, la Fondazione ha sviluppato un programma espositivo che mette in relazione linguaggi e pubblici differenti, articolandosi tra il Piano Nobile, la Strozzina e il Cortile, con un progetto istituzionale che fondato sulla collaborazione tra soggetti pubblici e privati. Nel corso di due decenni, ha dato vita a grandi mostre e progetti artistici di livello internazionale, attraversando la storia dell’arte dal Rinascimento alle ricerche più recenti, e facendo del confronto tra patrimonio storico e contemporaneità uno degli assi della propria programmazione.

«La Fondazione Palazzo Strozzi nasce da una scelta lungimirante: unire istituzioni pubbliche e soggetti privati in un progetto culturale capace di generare valore per Firenze. In vent’anni questo modello ha contribuito a rafforzare il ruolo internazionale della città, creando nuove opportunità di partecipazione e sviluppo. Oggi rinnoviamo il nostro impegno a rendere Palazzo Strozzi un’istituzione sempre più aperta e parte integrante della vita culturale e civica di Firenze», ha dichiarato Luigi De Siervo.

I numeri restituiscono le dimensioni di questo percorso: oltre settanta mostre realizzate, più di 500 opere ospitate, collaborazioni con oltre 100 musei e istituzioni in tutto il mondo e più di tre milioni di visitatori. Tra le esposizioni dedicate all’arte antica figurano quelle rivolte a maestri come Beato Angelico , Donatello , Andrea del Verrocchio , Pontormo , Rosso Fiorentino e Bronzino . Accanto a questi progetti, la Fondazione ha presentato mostre dedicate a nomi come Pablo Picasso e Mark Rothko , e ancora Ai Weiwei , Marina Abramović , Olafur Eliasson e Tracey Emin . Questa alternanza tra periodi storici e pratiche artistiche abbraccia anche il modo in cui Palazzo Strozzi utilizza i propri spazi: il Cortile, in particolare, si è consolidato come il luogo in cui l’intervento contemporaneo entra in relazione diretta con l’architettura del palazzo e con la città, portando l’arte fuori dai confini tradizionali delle sale espositive.

Accanto alla programmazione espositiva, la Fondazione ha sviluppato attività rivolte a scuole, università, famiglie, giovani e adulti, con particolare attenzione all’accessibilità e alla partecipazione culturale. I programmi educativi e le iniziative dedicate alle persone con disabilità e ai pubblici a rischio di esclusione fanno parte di un lavoro che considera la fruizione dell’arte anche in relazione alle condizioni e alle esigenze dei diversi visitatori.

«Celebrare vent’anni di Fondazione Palazzo Strozzi significa riaffermare una visione culturale che guarda al futuro. Abbiamo costruito un’identità fondata sulla qualità dei progetti espositivi, sulla ricerca e sul dialogo con i più importanti musei e artisti del mondo. In una città dal patrimonio straordinario come Firenze, la nostra ambizione è continuare a fare di Palazzo Strozzi uno spazio vivo di creazione e sperimentazione, protagonista del dibattito culturale contemporaneo», ha affermato Arturo Galansino.

article_text:
There is nary a time and place without financial concerns, but it’s well within the needs of any public-facing institution to maintain the image of strong, steady organization. Takeo Hisamatsu was appointed director of the Tokyo International Film Festival in April, resuming a title he held from 2017 to 2021 while inheriting some massive responsibilities for his nation’s cinema. As UniJapan’s vice president and former decision-maker at Warner Bros. Japan and Shochiku, he seems to appreciate the ever-evolving and never-quite-at-rest. Speaking to myself and four other journalists in Ginza’s posh Midtown Hibiya, Hisamatsu was extremely straight-faced about the challenges facing TIFF at a time when basic questions of authorship and autonomy—a question of basic humanity—are plaguing the film industry. Safe to say there is always the need for more money, and TIFF is staring down a 40th edition they hope to make a bigger-than-usual celebration.

To his credit, the 39th year maintains a strong surface, continuing TIFF’s habit of housing numerous films that are either world-premiering or have yet to make a significant dent since debuts at other, larger gatherings. In three years’ attendance I’ve especially appreciated their emphasis on Asian (particularly Japanese) features less-than-likely to receive any stateside play. It’s consistent with Hisamatsu’s desire to see more institutional support for local cinema, but a somewhat tricky line to tread when recent competition winners come from outside—our conversation was days before the top prize went to Sister Brother Manhole Cover , a film that boasts six countries in its credits, none Japanese—and programs like Asian Future make a point of defining “Asian cinema” more broadly than Japan, Korea, China, and Hong Kong. I asked Hisamatsu for his wider thoughts on the matter, to which he responded:

“Given the current circumstances for international film festivals, it’s important to take a path between introducing foreign films to Japanese moviegoers [and] at the same time, that Japanese films to be [brought] to overseas movie fans. So we need to have both. But in terms of the balance, I look to put more emphasis on introducing Japanese films, or filmmakers, to the world. Because we are part of the film industry. I’m surprised that, this year, some international film festivals, they screen a lot of, you know, Korean films. They say ‘we are global,’ but you know, if we do the same thing—competing against Cannes or Berlin or Venice—I don’t think that’s the right way we should go. So as we are in this country—the culture, the people, the filmmakers—I think it’s obvious, or it’s natural, to put more emphasis on your own country’s films and filmmakers to introduce to the world. That’s how I think.”

Still, the money. While one can look at TIFF’s impressive list of sponsors—a globalized consortium boasting Rolex (which has made a massive push in recent years to support Sundance, NYFF, TIFF), likewise-major entities (Coca-Cola, Capcom, Bandai Namco, Morgan Stanley), and more regional groups—and grasp a job well done, Hisamatsu tells us nothing is guaranteed (or easy to plan) when government funds change every year. His preference: a certain amount is promised for at least two or three years à la athlete contracts. Which is not even accounting for more or less nothing getting cheaper nowadays (he noted airline tickets as a particular culprit) and few with wallets to open factoring art-in-hard-times bromides when deciding where to actually put the cash. (As one who appreciates round-trip flights to Tokyo and chance to witness something at least a bit unique in the increasingly homogenized film scene, I know where my hopes lie.) Hisamatsu was also insistent that film festivals aren’t festive enough. Where music festivals fulfill the concept of a large gathering by degrees and in, multiple senses, volume, why, he asks, can’t there be a balance between the serious act of watching movies in dark, quiet rooms and celebrating said movies and their makers in the immediate vicinity? The thinking has me hopeful for next year’s 40th-anniversary edition, about which during my week in Ginza I heard more than one intimation of aims for a bigger-than-usual celebration of Japanese cinema’s expansive history.

It’s fair to surmise that some greater sense of community would aid these efforts. To wit, Hisamatsu boasted of a party he’d host that evening for numerous Japanese filmmakers—on the one hand a social gathering natural to the festival environment and on the other his hope to ameliorate a lack of proper socializing in local film circles. This sparked my curiosity as to what most concerns local directors at a time when—here as elsewhere—money and AI hang like a black cloud. I did not expect the answer to be “English education,” but as he elaborated:

“Honestly. You know, in this country, English class starts from junior high school. I spent three years, in high school three years, and in college four years. So: ten years we learned English. Still, we still can’t speak English. That’s a problem. We have to change our education system. And English is the key. Fortunately for you—unfortunately for us—we have to spend more time to learn English. Maybe more words or something. It’s a handicap for us. But, you know, to communicate with other people in this given world, whether you like it or not, you have to speak English, right? And if you can speak English, you can communicate with more people around the world. European people, they speak English very well—like French people, Dutch people. The English alphabet may be much closer than us. For them, probably, it’s easier to speak English than us. So you can communicate in English easily. But for us, that’s like a handicap. But don’t complain; do something. Right?”

As Kenji Ishizaka told me just a day prior and Academy CEO Bill Kramer elaborated in his own TIFF panel, the windows between eastern and western industries are closing, while no less a figure than Kiyoshi Kurosawa and Ryusuke Hamaguchi told me that recent expeditions in France could be their stepping stone to an American debut. I don’t expect either to become fluent in English—one more readily imagines producers surrounding them with expert interpreters, even actors (à la Virginie Efira) learning for themselves—but I see the overlap. American cinema simply doesn’t have enough good filmmakers that it can afford to let the opportunity for cross-hemisphere exchange fall through the cracks. Should it come to pass sometime soon, support from the Tokyo International Film Festival and Hisamatsu will likely become part of that history.

Source: Tomo Brejc / Good Chaos

Ṣọpé Dìrísù, Edem Kelman

EXCLUSIVE: Production has wrapped on Edem Kelman’s debut feature Chairman starring Ṣọpé Dìrísù following a shoot in London and Paris.

Dìrísù plays Duke, a man who dreams of uniting London’s African diasporic community. As his ambition grows, so do the risks, endangering not only his dreams but also the lives of those who come to rely on him.

Samuel Adewunmi and Heather Agyepong star alongside Dìrísù.

Chairman is based on an idea by Kelman, who co-wrote the script with Noah Reich. Reich produces for his Two by Two Productions, with James Bowsher and Mike Goodridge for Good Chaos. Sydney Oberfeld is a co-producer for Good Chaos.

The film was developed by Film4, and is co-financed by Film4, the BFI (awarding National Lottery funding), HiPo Productions, Amplify Capital, Head Gear Films, Metrol Technology and Bleat Film.

Executive producers are David Kimbangi for Film4, Ama Ampadu for the BFI, Nick Potts and Jessica Hickman for HiPo, Demola Elebute for Amplify Capital, Phil Hunt and Compton Ross for Head Gear, and Tristin Norwell and David Turner for Bleat.

Key heads of department include cinematographer David Gallego, production designer Phoebe Platman, costume designer Ruka Johnson, hair and makeup designer Billie McKenzie, casting director Coralie Rose, line producer Rob Jelley, first assistant director Jay Farrall-Miles and editor Fin Oates.

Kelman was named a Screen UK-Ireland Star of Tomorrow in 2021, and has previously made shorts including 2022’s Express, while 2025’s Terence was nominated for the Bafta for best British short film. Dìrísù and Adewunmi were also named Stars of Tomorrow in 2016 and 2019, as was Bowsher in 2024.

“With an electric Ṣọpé Dìrísù at its heart, the film promises to be a soulful, fearless, and ambitious debut that brings a whole community vividly to life,” said Kimbangi, with Film4 having previously backed Express .

Source: Tayler Prince-Fraser / David Reiss

Samuel Adewunmi, Heather Agyepong

“With its vivid, propulsive style, the film immerses us in the world of first-generation African diasporic communities in the UK,” said Ampadu. “ Chairman feels particularly timely, speaking to the experience of displacement while exploring the fundamental human need for belonging and community.”

Interview

Jonathan Nez on Indigenous Perseverance

The former Navajo Nation president running for Congress in Arizona speaks to Hyperallergic about his upbringing, how Diné culture shapes his political thinking, and the importance of historical memory.

This November, Jonathan Nez could become the first Native American to represent Arizona in Congress. Nez, who served as president of the Navajo Nation from 2019 to 2023, is running to flip the state's largest congressional district by area, a seat currently held by Republican Eli Crane. His “ Warrior Up ” platform is structured into four pillars, a tribute to the number's significance to Diné people, for whom the world is bound by four sacred mountains , one in each cardinal direction.

Nez has campaigned on lowering healthcare and housing costs, building sustainable rural infrastructure, tackling corruption in Washington, and the belief that “water is life and food is medicine.” In Arizona, where long-term drought and water supplies strain the Colorado River, one in three Diné households lack access to clean water.

As the Trump administration continues to roll back protections for Native land and sacred sites, Nez’s perspective feels especially urgent. A few days before Indigenous Peoples’ Day, we spoke about his upbringing, how Diné culture shapes his political thinking, and the importance of historical memory in fostering perseverance and resistance.

On the day of our interview, a Trump-aligned Political Action Committee (PAC) ran ad against Nez that mistakenly used a photograph of a different Navajo leader (ironically, a Republican supporter). The PAC acknowledged the mistake and corrected the ad, but the egregious error illustrates the political climate in which Nez is campaigning, as well as the continued discrimination against Indigenous people in the United States. The interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

Hyperallergic: You were born on the Navajo Reservation and raised in Shonto, a small Navajo community in northeastern Arizona. Can you tell me a little bit about what your upbringing was like?

Jonathan Nez: I grew up in a very small community, Shonto, where we lived without running water or electricity. There's a lot of folks, including my wife, who grew up that way. But we had livestock, we had our farms, and so it was an upbringing of hard work: tending to our animals, herding sheep, herding cattle, riding horses, going to the farms, getting our food — getting the corn from the farm, starting a fire, and roasting the corn on an open flame while we're tending to our livestock. Those were fun days. We didn't know that was a hard upbringing, right? We were just growing up, and that's what was expected of us. I say that because it has shaped who I am today. And I think over my 20-plus years in public service, I have worked hard and gotten things done because of my upbringing.

I grew up in a very conservative home. Both parents Republican, sitting in a Baptist church early on, but at the same time knowing who I am as a Navajo. I'm a Democrat today, but my parents instilled in us, my brothers and sisters, a bootstrap mentality to do things for yourself. There was always that challenge from our elders, my parents and the elders in the community, to go get an education and get a job outside the Nation, to get that experience. And to come home with that experience to help your community, your people, your Nation.

My wife and I did that. We went home, and I got elected at an early age, in my mid-20s, to the local community government, then became a lawmaker, a council member of the Navajo Nation. I also got elected twice to the county Board of Supervisors, the equivalent of a county commissioner, which gave me a better understanding of county and state relations. I became the vice president and the president of the largest Indian tribe in the country, which gave me a better understanding of working with the federal government one-on-one.

Cine

FICM 2026: La bola negra – Crítica de la película

Andrea Alejandra

Una dirección fenomenal.

Lo más importante de la vida es vivir. Suena obvio, pero en la práctica raramente lo es. Sobre todo porque el ser humano es una criatura muy curiosa a la que se le da por ponerse obstáculos. Obstáculos representados en forma de prejuicios, guerras, represión. Pero no es que estemos condenados, porque al mismo tiempo hay quienes tienen la valentía de crear y de expresar, y, por consiguiente, vivir. La bola negra es una película que surge de ese tipo de valentía, y de la necesidad de acabar cosas inacabadas, de decir cosas no dichas.

Éste largometraje tuvo su estreno en el pasado festival de Cannes. Le dio el premio a Mejor Dirección a sus realizadores, Javier Ambrossi y Javier Calvo. La trama está inspirada en La piedra oscura , obra de teatro escrita por Alberto Conejero. Y también en La bola negra , obra de teatro que Federico García Lorca comenzó a escribir, pero no pudo terminar porque fue asesinado.

La historia entrelaza la vida de tres hombres homosexuales en diferentes periodos. Sebastián, un músico que por trágicas circunstancias se convierte en miembro del ejército fascista durante la guerra civil española. Carlos, un chico presionado por su padre a esconder su orientación sexual y a encajar con el resto de la sociedad. Y Alberto, un ex-escritor de obras teatrales que descubre un secreto familiar tras la muerte de su abuelo.

¿Dónde puedes ver La bola negra y otros estrenos del FICM? Entérate aquí.

El reconocimiento que Calvo y Ambrossi se llevaron en Cannes es totalmente merecido. Su dirección logra sumergirnos en la historia y reforzar cada una de las temáticas que aborda. Combinan exitosamente una bella fotografía y una estruendosa música, en secuencias que van desde lo más crudo hasta lo onírico, Y los movimientos de cámara acompañan a los actores como si fueran pareja de baile.

Pero lo que más exuda La bola negra es sensualidad y tragedia. La sensualidad llega cuando la cámara navega por la piel de sus protagonistas, acompañando su sudor y su aliento lentamente. Y la tragedia impacta al reflexionar que este tipo de historias funcionan, muchas veces, como la única conclusión para historias de amor reprimidas.

Claro que, sin caer en el pesimismo, el largometraje también recuerda que la importancia de este tipo de producciones recae en que, como lo expresa la misma película, pueden servirle a nuevas generaciones para que no cometan los mismos errores y no acaben en las mismas circunstancias. Una nota esperanzadora al final del tortuoso camino.

La bola negra es un ejercicio que nos invita a revisitar la historia, poniendo el énfasis en las personas que la construyeron, y lo que nos hace sentir, más que los hechos.

Andrea Alejandra El cine es mi pasión y hablar sobre este es mi vocación.
